say: You give it a triangle where some angles or sides are unknown. It tells you which side is the **longest** and which angle is the **greatest**.
The key idea: the greater angle always faces the greater side. It works the other way round too, so the longest side faces the greatest angle.

example.question: In triangle $ABC$, $|\angle A| = (x + 30)^\circ$, $|\angle B| = (2x - 10)^\circ$ and $|\angle C| = (3x - 20)^\circ$. Find $x$, and name the longest side of the triangle.

steps.title: Add the three angles
steps.say: The angles of a triangle add to $180^\circ$. Write that as an equation and collect the terms.

steps.title: Solve for x
steps.say: Divide both sides by $6$ to find $\hl{1}{x}$.

steps.title: Use Theorem 7
steps.say: Theorem 7: the greater angle is opposite the greater side. The greatest angle is $\hl{2}{70^\circ}$ at $C$, so the longest side is the one opposite $C$.

say: You give it three lengths, or two lengths and an unknown third. It tells you whether a triangle can be made, and how long the unknown side can be.
The key idea: any two sides together must be **longer** than the third. If they are not, the two sides cannot reach each other.

how.ordinary: At Ordinary level it turned up once in 11 years, as a 5 mark part of a Paper 2 construction question: pick the triangle that can be drawn and give a reason.

example.question: A triangle has two sides of length $6$ cm and $9$ cm. The third side is $x$ cm, where $x$ is a whole number. How many different values can $x$ have?

steps.title: Find the largest x
steps.say: Theorem 8: two sides together are longer than the third. The two given sides must together be longer than $\hl{1}{x}$.

steps.title: Find the smallest x
steps.say: Now $6$ and $\hl{1}{x}$ together must be longer than $9$.

lines.text: The third pair, $9 + x > 6$, is true for every $x$ here.

steps.title: List the whole numbers
steps.say: $x$ is between $3$ and $15$, and not equal to either. The whole numbers are $4, 5, \dots, 14$. Count them.

ordinary.tip: Name the triangle and give the reason. Either one alone only earns part of the marks.
The reason is about the sides: the two shorter ones are not long enough to meet.

say: You give it a right-angled triangle with two sides known. It finds the third side.
The key idea: the square on the **hypotenuse** (the side opposite the right angle) equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.
what.in: two sides of a right angle

how.higher: At Higher level it is a step inside bigger questions, mostly on Paper 2 (solids, circles, trigonometry), and once on Paper 1 in an equation. It was the main skill in 5 parts over 11 years, worth 5 to 15 marks.
how.ordinary: At Ordinary level it is usually a part of its own on Paper 2, worth 10 marks. It was the main skill in 4 parts over 11 years.

example.question: A ladder $7{\cdot}4$ m long leans against a vertical wall. The foot of the ladder is $2{\cdot}1$ m from the wall. How high up the wall does the ladder reach? Give your answer correct to one decimal place.

steps.title: Find the hypotenuse
steps.say: The wall is vertical and the ground is flat, so there is a right angle between them. The ladder is opposite the right angle, so it is the hypotenuse.

lines.text: Write Pythagoras: hypotenuse$^2$ = sum of the other two sides squared.

steps.title: Substitute into Pythagoras
steps.say: Let $\hl{1}{h}$ be the height up the wall. Put the numbers in.

steps.title: Solve for h squared
steps.say: Take $2{\cdot}1^2$ from both sides to get $h^2$ on its own.

steps.title: Take the square root
steps.say: Square root both sides, then round to one decimal place.

higher.tip: Write Pythagoras with the numbers in it. Fully substituting is a step the marks are tied to.
If you are stuck, still write Pythagoras down. Any use of it earns partial credit.
Put the unit on a length. Leaving it off, or using the wrong one, costs a mark.

sources.quote: Apply a * for incorrect or no unit

ordinary.tip: Write the theorem down first. Writing Pythagoras is itself worth marks.
Substitute every number into the formula. A fully substituted formula earns the next band of marks.
Finding the square is not the end. Take the square root to finish.
Give the unit and round as asked. Each one costs a mark if missed.

sources.quote: Correct answer, no unit or incorrect unit

say: You give it a triangle with all three sides known. It tells you whether the triangle has a **right angle**.
The key idea: if the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two, the angle opposite the longest side is $90^\circ$.

how.higher: At Higher level it turned up once in 11 years, as a 5 mark part on Paper 1: show that a set of three sides satisfies Pythagoras.

example.question: A triangle has sides of length $20$ cm, $99$ cm and $101$ cm. Show that the triangle is right-angled.

steps.title: Pick the longest side
steps.say: If there is a right angle, it is opposite the longest side, so that side is the hypotenuse. Here it is $\hl{1}{101}$.

lines.text: Test: does the sum of the other two squares equal $101^2$?

steps.title: Square the short sides
steps.say: Square the two shorter sides and add them.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.say: The two results are equal. By the converse of Pythagoras (Theorem 15), the angle opposite the longest side is a right angle.

higher.tip: Write out each square and the sum, with both sides shown equal. Do not just state that it works.
